title: Nonuniqueness of Weak Solutions to the Navier-Stokes Equation

# Nonuniqueness of weak solutions to the Navier-Stokes equation

# Abstract

For initial datum of finite kinetic energy, Leray has proven in 1934 that there exists at least one global in time finite energy weak solution of the 3D Navier-Stokes equations. In this paper we prove that weak solutions of the 3D Navier-Stokes equations are not unique in the class of weak solutions with finite kinetic energy. Moreover, we prove that Hölder continuous dissipative weak solutions of the 3D Euler equations may be obtained as a strong vanishing viscosity limit of a sequence of finite energy weak solutions of the 3D Navier-Stokes equations.

# 1 Introduction

In this paper we consider the 3D incompressible Navier-Stokes equation

$$\begin{align*}
\partial_t v + {\mathrm{div\,}}(v \otimes v) + \nabla p -  {\nu}\Delta v &=0 \tag{1}\\
{\mathrm{div\,}}v &= 0 \tag{2}\end{align*}$$

posed on ${\mathbb{T}}^3\times {\mathbb{R}}$, with periodic boundary conditions in $x\in\mathbb T^3=\mathbb R^3 / 2\pi\mathbb Z^3$. We consider solutions normalized to have zero spatial mean, i.e., $\int_{{\mathbb{T}}^3} v(x,t) dx = 0$. The constant $\nu \in (0,1]$ is the kinematic viscosity. We define weak solutions to the Navier-Stokes equations (Serrin63, Definition 1), (FabesJonesRiviere72, pp. 226):

As a direct result of the work of Fabes-Jones-Riviere (FabesJonesRiviere72), since the weak solutions defined above lie in $C^0({\mathbb{R}};L^2({\mathbb{T}}^3))$, they are in fact solutions of the integral form of the Navier-Stokes equations

$$\begin{align*}
v(\cdot,t) = e^{\nu t  \Delta} v(\cdot,0) + \int_0^t  e^{\nu (t-s)\Delta}{\mathbb{P}}{\mathrm{div\,}}(v(\cdot,s)\otimes v(\cdot,s)) ds \, , \tag{3}\end{align*}$$

and are sometimes called *mild* or *Oseen* solutions (cf. (FabesJonesRiviere72) and (Lemarie16, Definition 6.5)). Here ${\mathbb{P}}$ is the Leray projector and $e^{t\Delta}$ denotes convolution with the heat kernel.

## 1.1 Previous works

In (Leray34), Leray considered the Cauchy-problem for (1) for initial datum of finite kinetic energy, $v_0 \in L^2$. Leray proved that for any such datum, there exists a global in time weak solution $v \in L^\infty_t L^2_x$, which additionally has the regularity $L^2_t \dot{H}^1_x$, and obeys the energy inequality $\left\|v(t)\right\|_{L^2}^2 + 2 \nu \int_0^t \left\|\nabla u(s)\right\|_{L^2}^2 ds \leq \left\|v_0\right\|_{L^2}^2$. Hopf (Hopf51) established a similar result for the equations posed in a smooth bounded domain, with Dirichlet boundary conditions. To date, the question of uniqueness of Leray-Hopf weak solutions for the 3D Navier-Stokes equations remains however open.

Based on the natural scaling of the equations $v(x,t) \mapsto v_\lambda(x,t) = \lambda v(\lambda x,\lambda^2 t)$, a number of partial regularity results have been established (Scheffer76; CaffarelliKohnNirenberg82; Lin98; LadyzhenskayaSeregin99; Vasseur07; Kukavica08b); the local existence for the Cauchy problem has been proven in scaling-invariant spaces (Kato84; KochTataru01; JiaSverak14); and conditional regularity has been established under geometric structure assumptions (ConstantinFefferman93) or assuming a signed pressure (SereginSverak02). The conditional regularity and weak-strong uniqueness results known under the umbrella of Ladyzhenskaya-Prodi-Serrin conditions (KiselevLadyzhenskaya57; Prodi59; Serrin62), state that if a Leray-Hopf weak solution also lies in $L^p_t L^q_x$, with $\tfrac 2p + \tfrac 3q \leq 1$, then the solution is unique and smooth in positive time. These conditions and their generalizations have culminated with the work of Escauriaza-Seregin-Šverák (EscauriazaSerginSverak03) who proved the $L^\infty_t L^3_x$ endpoint. The uniqueness of mild/Oseen solutions is also known under the Ladyzhenskaya-Prodi-Serrin conditions, cf. (FabesJonesRiviere72) for $p>3$, and (FurioliLemarieRieussetTerraneo00; LionsMasmoudi01; LemarieRieusset02; Kukavica06b) for $p=3$. Note that the regularity of Leray-Hopf weak solutions, or of bounded energy weak solutions, is consistent with the scaling $\tfrac 2p + \tfrac 3q = \tfrac 32$. In contrast, the additional regularity required to ensure that the energy equality holds in the Navier-Stokes equations is consistent with $\tfrac 24 + \tfrac 34 = \tfrac 54$ for $p=q=4$ (Shinbrot74; Kukavica06). See (ConstantinFoias88; Temam01; LemarieRieusset02; RSR16; Lemarie16) for surveys of results on the Navier-Stokes equations.

The gap between the scaling of the kinetic energy and the natural scaling of the equations leaves open the possibility of nonuniqueness of weak solutions to (1). In (JiaSverak14; JiaSverak15) Jia-Šverák proved that non-uniqueness of Leray-Hopf weak solutions in the regularity class $L^\infty_t L^{3,\infty}_x$ holds if a certain spectral assumption holds for a linearized Navier-Stokes operator. While a rigorous proof of this spectral condition remains open, very recently Guillod-Šverák (GuillodSverak17) have provided compelling numerical evidence of it, using a scenario related to the example of Ladyzhenskaya (Ladyzhenskaya67). Thus, the works (JiaSverak15; GuillodSverak17) strongly suggest that the Ladyzhenskaya-Prodi-Serrin regularity criteria are sharp.

## 1.2 Main results

In this paper we prove that weak solutions to (1) (in the sense of Definition 1) are not unique within the class of weak solutions with bounded kinetic energy. We establish the stronger result[^1]:

In particular, the above theorem shows that $v \equiv 0$ is not the only weak solution which vanishes at a time slice, thereby implying the nonuniqueness of weak solutions. Theorem 1.2 shows that weak solutions may come to rest in finite time, a question posed by Serrin (Serrin63, pp. 88). Moreover, by considering $e_1(t),e_2(t)> 0$ which are nonincreasing, such that $e_1(t)= e_2(t)$ for $t\in[0,\tfrac{T}{2}]$, and $e_1(T)<e_2(T)$, the construction used to prove Theorem 1.2 also proves the nonuniqueness of dissipative weak solutions.

From the proof of Theorem 1.2 it is clear that the constructed weak solutions $v$ also have regularity in time, i.e. there exists $\gamma>0$ such that $v \in C^\gamma_t ([0,T]; L^2_x(\mathbb T^3))$. Thus, $v\otimes v$ lies in $C^{\gamma}_t L^{1}_x \cap C^0_t L^{1+\gamma}_x$, and the fact that $\nabla v \in C^0_t L^1_x$ follows from (3) and the maximal regularity of the heat equation.

We note that while the weak solutions Theorem 1.2 may attain any smooth energy profile, at the moment we do not prove that they are Leray-Hopf weak solutions, i.e., they do not obey the energy inequality or have $L^2_t \dot{H}^{1}_x$ integrability. Moreover, the regularity parameter $\beta>0$ cannot be expected to be too large, since at $\beta = \tfrac 12$ one has weak-strong uniqueness (ConstantinFoias88). We expect that the ideas used to prove Theorem 1.2 will in the future lead to a proof of nonuniqueness of weak solutions in $C^0_t L^p_x$, for any $2\leq p<3$, and the nonuniqueness of Leray-Hopf weak solutions.

The proof of Theorem 1.2 builds on several of the fundamental ideas pioneered by De Lellis-Székelyhidi Jr. (DLSZ09; DLSZ13). These ideas were used to tackle the Onsager conjecture for the Euler equation (Eyink94; ConstantinETiti94; ChCoFrSh2008) (set $\nu = 0$ in (1)) via convex integration methods (Scheffer93; Shnirelman97; BDLISJ15; DLSZ15; Buckmaster15; BDLSZ16), leading to the resolution of the conjecture by Isett (Isett16; Isett17), using a key ingredient by Daneri and Székelyhidi Jr. (DSZ17). The construction of dissipative Euler solutions below the Onsager regularity threshold was proven by authors of this paper jointly with De Lellis and Székelyhidi Jr. in (BDLSV17), building on the ideas in (DSZ17; Isett16). In order to treat the dissipative term $-\nu \Delta$, not present in the Euler system, we cannot proceed as in (BSV16; CDLDR17), since in these works Hölder continuous weak solutions are constructed, which is possible only by using building blocks which are sparse in the frequency variable and for small fractional powers of the Laplacian. Instead, the main idea, which is also used in (BMV17), is to use building blocks for the convex integration scheme which are “intermittent”. That is, the building blocks we use are spatially inhomogeneous, and have different scaling in different $L^p$ norms. At high frequency, these building blocks attempt to saturate the Bernstein inequalities from Littlewood-Paley theory. Since they are built by adding eigenfunctions of ${\mathrm{curl\,}}$ in a certain geometric manner, we call these building blocks *intermittent Beltrami flows*. In particular, the proof of Theorem 1.2 breaks down in $2D$, as is expected, since there are not enough spatial directions to oscillate in. The proof of Theorem 1.2 is given in Section 2 below.

The idea of using intermittent building blocks can be traced back to classical observations in hydrodynamic turbulence, see for instance (Frisch95). Moreover, in view of the aforementioned works on the Onsager conjecture for the Euler equations, we are naturally led to consider the set of accumulation points in the vanishing viscosity limit $\nu \to 0$ of the family of weak solutions to the Navier-Stokes equations which we constructed in Theorem 1.2. We prove in this paper that this set of accumulation points, in the $C^0_t L^2_x$ topology, contains all the Hölder continuous weak solutions of the 3D Euler equations:

In particular, Theorem 1.2 shows that the nonconservative weak solutions to the Euler equations obtained in (Isett16; BDLSV17) arise in the vanishing viscosity limit of weak solutions to the Navier-Stokes equations. Thus, being a strong limit of weak solutions to the Navier-Stokes equations, in the sense of Definition 1, cannot serve as a selection criterion for weak solutions of the Euler equation. Whether similar vanishing viscosity results hold for sequences of Leray-Hopf weak solutions, or for suitable weak solutions of (1), remains a challenging open problem. The proof of Theorem 1.2 is closely related to that of Theorem 1.2, and is also given in Section 2 below.

# 2 Outline of the convex integration scheme

In this section we sketch the proof of Theorem 1.2. For every integer $q \geq 0$ we will construct a solution $(v_q,p_q, \mathring R_q)$ to the Navier-Stokes-Reynolds system

$$\begin{align*}
\partial_t v_q + {\mathrm{div\,}}(v_q\otimes v_q)+\nabla p_q - \nu \Delta v_q &= {\mathrm{div\,}}\mathring R_q \tag{4}\\
{\mathrm{div\,}}v_q &= 0\, . \tag{5}\end{align*}$$

where the Reynolds stress $\mathring R_q$ is assumed to be a trace-free symmetric matrix.

## 2.1 Parameters

Throughout the proof we fix a sufficiently large, universal constant $b \in 16{\mathbb{N}}$, and depending on $b$ we fix a regularity parameter $\beta>0$ such that $\beta b^2\leq 4$ and $\beta b \leq \tfrac{1}{40}$. We remark that it is sufficient to take $b = 2^9$ and $\beta = 2^{-16}$.

The relative size of the approximate solution $v_q$ and the Reynolds stress error $\mathring R_q$ will be measured in terms of a frequency parameter $\lambda_q$ and an amplitude parameter $\delta_q$ defined as

$$\begin{align*}
\lambda_{q} &=   a^{(b^q)}  \\
\delta_{q} &= \lambda_1^{3\beta} \lambda_{q}^{-2\beta}
\end{align*}$$

for some integer $a  \gg 1$ to be chosen suitably.

## 2.2 Inductive estimates

By induction, we will assume the following estimates[^2] on the solution of (2) at level $q$:

$$\begin{align*}
\left\|v_q\right\|_{C^1_{x,t}}&\leq \lambda_{q}^4 \tag{6}\\
\left\|\mathring R_{q}\right\|_{L^{1}} &\leq \lambda_q^{-\varepsilon_R}\delta_{q+1} \tag{7}\\
\left\|\mathring R_{q}\right\|_{C^1_{x,t}} &\leq \lambda_{q}^{10}
\, . \tag{8}\end{align*}$$

We additionally assume

$$0 \leq e(t) - \int_{\mathbb T^3}\left|v_q\right|^2~dx\leq  \delta_{q+1} \tag{9}$$

and

$$e(t) - \int_{\mathbb T^3}\left| v_q(x,t)\right|^2~dx\leq  \frac{\delta_{q+1}}{100}~\Rightarrow  v_q(\cdot,t) \equiv 0 \quad \mbox{and} \quad \mathring R_q(\cdot,t)\equiv 0 \, . \tag{10}$$

for all $t\in [0,T]$.

## 2.3 The main proposition and iterative procedure

In addition to the sufficiently large universal constant $b$, and the sufficiently small regularity parameter $\beta = \beta(b)>0$ fixed earlier, we fix the constant $M_e = \left\|e\right\|_{C^1_t}$. The following iteration lemma states the existence of a solution of (2) at level $q+1$, which obeys suitable bounds.

The principal new idea in the proof of Proposition 2.3 is to construct the perturbation $v_{q+1}-v_{q}$ as a sum of terms of the form

$$\begin{align*}

a_{(\xi)}\mathbb W_{(\xi)} \tag{11}\end{align*}$$

where $\mathbb W_{(\xi)}$ is an intermittent Beltrami wave (cf. (25) below) with frequency support centered at frequency $\xi\lambda_{q+1}$ for $\xi\in\mathbb S^2$. While these intermittent Beltrami waves have similar properties (cf. Proposition 3.2) to the usual Beltrami flows used in the previous convex integration constructions (DLSZ13; BDLISJ15; DLSZ15; Buckmaster15; BDLSZ16) for the Euler equations, they are fundamentally different since their $L^1$ norm is much smaller than their $L^2$ norm (cf. Proposition 3.2). The gain comes from the fact that the Reynolds stress has to be estimated in $L^1$ rather than $L^2$, and that the term $\nu \Delta v$ is linear in $v$. At the technical level, one difference with respect to (Isett16; BDLSV17) is the usage of very large gaps between consecutive frequency parameters (i.e., $b\gg 1$), which is consistent with a small regularity parameter $\beta$. Next, we show that Proposition 2.3 implies the main theorems of the paper.

## 2.4 Proof of Theorem 1.2

Choose all the parameters from the statement of Proposition 2.3, except for $a$, which we may need to be larger (so that it is still larger than $a_0$).

For $q=0$ we note that the identically zero solution trivially satisfies (2) with $\mathring R_0= 0$, and the inductive assumptions (6), (7), and (8) hold. Moreover, by taking $a$ sufficiently large such that it is in the range of Proposition 2.3 (i.e. $a \geq a_0$) we may ensure that

$$\begin{equation*}
|e(t)| \leq \left\|e\right\|_{C^1_t} = M_e \leq  \frac{\lambda_1^\beta }{100} = \frac{\delta_{1}}{100}.
\end{equation*}$$

Then the zero solution also satisfies (9) and (10).

For $q \geq 1$ we inductively apply Proposition 2.3. The bound (2.3) and interpolation implies[^3]

$$\begin{align*}
\sum_{q=0}^{\infty} \left\|v_{q+1}-v_q\right\|_{H^{\beta'}} 
&\lesssim \; \sum_{q=0}^{\infty} \left\|v_{q+1}-v_q\right\|_{L^{2}}^{1-\beta'}(\left\|v_{q+1}\right\|_{C^1} + \left\|v_q\right\|_{C^{1}})^{\beta'} \\
&\lesssim \; \sum_{q=0}^{\infty}M^{1-\beta'}\lambda_1^{3\beta \frac{1-\beta'}{2}} \lambda_{q+1}^{- \beta \frac{1-\beta'}{2}}\lambda_{q+1}^{4\beta'}  \\
&\lesssim  M^{1-\beta'}\lambda_1^{3\beta \frac{1-\beta'}{2}} \, , \tag{12}\end{align*}$$

for $\beta'< \tfrac{\beta}{(8+\beta)}$, and hence the sequence $\{v_q\}_{q\geq 0}$ is uniformly bounded $C^0_t H^{\beta'}_x$, for such $\beta'$. Furthermore, by taking $a$ sufficiently large (depending on $b$, $\beta$ and $\beta'$) the implicit constant in (?) can be made to be universal. From (2), (7), the previously established uniform boundedness in $C_t^0 L^2_x$, and the embedding $W^{2,1}_x \subset L^2_x$ we obtain that

$$\begin{align*}
\left\|\partial_t v_q\right\|_{H^{-3}} 
&\lesssim\left\|{\mathbb{P}}{\mathrm{div\,}}(v_q \otimes v_q) - \nu \Delta v_q - {\mathbb{P}}{\mathrm{div\,}}\mathring R_q\right\|_{H^{-3}} \\
&\lesssim\left\|v_q \otimes v_q\right\|_{L^1} + \left\|v_q\right\|_{L^2} + \left\|\mathring R_q\right\|_{L^1}
\\
&\lesssim M^2\lambda_1^{3\beta}
\end{align*}$$

where ${\mathbb{P}}$ is the Leray projector. Thus, the sequence $\{v_q\}_{q\geq0}$ is uniformly bounded in $C^1_t H^{-3}_x$. It follows that for any $0< \beta'' < \beta'$ the sum

$$\begin{align*}
\sum_{q\geq 0} (v_{q+1}-v_{q}) =: v
\end{align*}$$

converges in $C^0_t H^{\beta''}_x$, and since $\left\|\mathring R_q\right\|_{L^1} \to 0$ as $q \to \infty$, $v$ is a $C^0_t H^{\beta''}_x$ weak solution of the Navier-Stokes equation. Lastly, in view of (9) we have that the kinetic energy of $v(\cdot,t)$ is given by $e(t)$ for all $t\in [0,T]$, concluding the proof of the theorem.

## 2.5 Proof of Theorem 1.2

Fix $\bar \beta >0$ and a weak solution $u \in C^{\bar \beta}_{t,x}$ to the Euler equation on $[-2T,2T]$. The existence of such solutions is guaranteed in view of the results of (Isett16; BDLSV17) for $\bar \beta < \tfrac 13$, and for $\bar \beta>1$ from the classical local existence results. Let $M_u = \left\|u\right\|_{C^{\bar \beta}}$. Pick an integer $n\geq 1$.

Choose all the parameters as in Proposition 2.3, except for $a\geq a_0$, which we may take even larger, depending also on $M_u$ and $\beta'$ which obeys $0< \beta' < \min(\tfrac{\bar \beta}{2} , \tfrac{\beta}{(8+\beta)})$. We make $a$ even larger, depending also on $\beta'$, so that in view of (?) we may ensure that

$$\begin{align*}
\sum_{q=n}^{\infty}M^{1-\beta'}\lambda_1^{3\beta \frac{1-\beta'}{2}} \lambda_{q+1}^{- \beta \frac{1-\beta'}{2}}\lambda_{q+1}^{4\beta'} \leq \frac{1}{2 C n} \tag{13}\end{align*}$$

where $C$ is the implicit constant in (?).

Let $\{ \phi_{\varepsilon} \}_{\varepsilon>0}$ be a family of standard compact support (of width $2$) Friedrichs mollifiers on ${\mathbb{R}}^3$ (space), and $\{\varphi_{\varepsilon}\}_{\varepsilon>0}$ be a family of standard compact support (of width $2$) Friedrichs mollifiers on ${\mathbb{R}}$ (time). We define

$$\begin{align*}
v_n = (u \ast_x \phi_{\lambda_n^{-1}}) \ast_t \varphi_{\lambda_n^{-1}}

\end{align*}$$

to be a mollification of $u$ in space and time, at length scale and time scale $\lambda_n^{-1}$, restricted to the temporal range $[0,T]$. Also, on $[0,T]$ define the energy function

$$\begin{align*}
e(t) = \int_{{\mathbb{T}}^3} |v_n(x,t)|^2 \, dx + \frac{\delta_n}{2}
\end{align*}$$

which ensures that (9) and (10) hold for $q=n$.

Since $u$ is a solution of the Euler equations, there exists a mean-free $p_n$ such that

$$\begin{align*}
\partial_t v_n + {\mathrm{div\,}}(v_n \otimes v_n) + \nabla p_n - \lambda_n^{-2} \Delta v_n = {\mathrm{div\,}}(\mathring R_n)
\end{align*}$$

where $\mathring R_n$ is the traceless symmetric part of the tensor

$$\begin{align*}

(v_n \otimes v_n) - ((u\otimes u)\ast_x \phi_{\lambda_n^{-1}}) \ast_t \varphi_{\lambda_n^{-1}} - \lambda_n^{-2}  \nabla v_n.
\end{align*}$$

Using a version of the commutator estimate introduced in (ConstantinETiti94), which may for instance be found in (CDLSJ12, Lemma 1), we obtain that

$$\begin{align*}
\left\|\mathring R_n\right\|_{L^1} \lesssim\left\|\mathring R_n\right\|_{C^0} \lesssim\lambda_n^{-1} M_u + \lambda_n^{-2\bar \beta} M_u^2 . \tag{14}\end{align*}$$

In addition, from a similar argument it follows that

$$\begin{align*}
\left\|\mathring R_n\right\|_{C^{1}_{t,x}} 
&\lesssim M_u + \lambda_n^{1-2\bar \beta } M_u^2 \tag{15}\\
\left\|v_n\right\|_{C^{1}_{t,x}} &\lesssim\lambda_n^{1-\bar \beta } M_u. \tag{16}\end{align*}$$

Setting

$$\nu:=\nu_n:=\lambda_n^{-1} \,,$$

then with $a$ sufficiently large, depending on $M_u$ and $\bar\beta$, we may ensure the pair $(v_n,\mathring R_n)$ obey the inductive assumptions (6)–(8) for $q=n$. Additionally, we may also choose $a$ sufficiently large, depending on $M_u$ and $\bar\beta$, so that

$$\begin{align*}
\lambda_n^{\bar \beta - \beta'} M_u \leq \frac{1}{2n |{\mathbb{T}}^3|^{\tfrac 12}}\,. \tag{17}\end{align*}$$

At this stage we may start the inductive Proposition 2.3, and as in the proof of Theorem 1.2, we obtain a weak solution $u^{(\nu_n)}$ of the Navier-Stokes equations, with the desired regularity, such that

$$\begin{align*}

\left\|v^{(\nu_n)} - u\right\|_{H^{\beta'}} \leq \left\|v^{(\nu_n)} - v_n\right\|_{H^{\beta'}} + |{\mathbb{T}}^3|^{\tfrac 12} \left\|u - v_n\right\|_{C^{\beta'}} \leq \frac{1}{n} \,.
\end{align*}$$

in view of (13) and (17). Since $n$ was arbitrary, this concludes the proof of the theorem.

# 3 Intermittent Beltrami Waves

In this section we will describe in detail the construction of the *intermittent Beltrami waves* which will form the building blocks of our convex integration scheme. Very roughly, intermittent Betrami waves are approximate Beltrami waves (approximate eigenfunctions to the curl operator) whose $L^1$ norm is significantly smaller than their $L^2$ norm.

## 3.1 Beltrami waves

We first recall from Proposition 3.1 and Lemma 3.2 in (DLSZ09) the construction of Beltrami waves (see also the summary given in (BDLISJ15)). In order to better suit our later goal of defining intermittent Beltrami waves, the statements of these propositions are slightly modified from the form they appear in (BDLISJ15), by making the substitution $\frac{k}{|k|} \mapsto \xi$.

## 3.2 Intermittent Beltrami waves

Recall cf. (GrafakosClassical, Section 3) that the Dirichlet kernel $D_n$ is defined as

$$D_n(x) = \sum_{\xi=-n}^n e^{i x \xi} = \frac{\sin((n+\tfrac12)x)}{\sin(x/2)} \tag{18}$$

and has the property that for any $p>1$ it obeys the estimate

$$\begin{align*}

\left\|D_n\right\|_{L^p} \sim n^{1-\tfrac{1}{p}}
\end{align*}$$

where the implicit constant only depends only on $p$. Replacing the sum in (18) by a sum of frequencies in a 3D integer cube

$$\Omega_{r}:=\Big\{\xi = (j,k,\ell) \colon j,k,\ell \in \{-r,\dots, r\} \Big\}$$

and normalizing to unit size in $L^2$, we obtain a kernel

$$D_{r}(x) :=\frac{1}{(2r+1)^{\tfrac{3}{2}}}\sum_{\xi\in \Omega_r} e^{i \xi \cdot x} = \frac{1}{(2r+1)^{\tfrac{3}{2}}}\sum_{j,k,\ell \in \{-r,\dots, r\} } e^{i (j x_1 + k x_2 + \ell x_3)}$$

such that for $1< p \leq \infty$ we have

$$\begin{align*}
\left\|D_{r}\right\|_{L^2}^2 = (2\pi)^3, 
\qquad \mbox{and} \qquad 
\left\|D_{r}\right\|_{L^p}\lesssim r^{\tfrac{3}{2}-\tfrac{3}{p}}\,, \tag{19}\end{align*}$$

where the implicit constant depends only on $p$. Note that $- \Omega_r = \Omega_r$.

The principal idea in the construction of intermittent Beltrami waves is to modify the Beltrami waves of the previous section by adding oscillations that mimic the structure of the kernels $D_{r}$ in order to construct approximate Beltrami waves with small $L^{p}$ norm for $p$ close to $1$. The large parameter *$r$ will parameterize the number of frequencies along edges of the cube* $\Omega_r$. We introduce a small parameter $\sigma$, such that $\lambda \sigma \in {\mathbb{N}}$ *parameterizes the spacing between frequencies*, or equivalently such that the resulting rescaled kernel is $(\tfrac{{\mathbb{T}}}{\lambda \sigma})^3$-periodic. We assume throughout the paper that

$$\sigma r \leq \tfrac{c_\Lambda}{(10 N_{\Lambda})} \,, \tag{20}$$

where $c_\Lambda \in (0,1)$ and $N_{\Lambda} \geq 1$ are the parameters from Remark 3.1. Lastly, we introduce a large parameter $\mu \in (\lambda, \lambda^2)$, which *measures the amount of temporal oscillation* in our building blocks. The parameters $\lambda, r, \sigma$ and $\mu$ are chosen in Section 4 below.

We recall from Propositions 3.1 and 3.1 that for $\xi \in \Lambda_\alpha$, the vectors $\{ \xi, A_\xi, \xi\times A_\xi\}$ form an orthonormal basis of ${\mathbb{R}}^3$, and by Remark 3.1 we have

$$N_{\Lambda} \xi, ~N_{\Lambda} A_\xi, ~N_{\Lambda} \xi \times A_\xi \in {\mathbb{Z}}^3\qquad \mbox{for all} \qquad \xi \in \Lambda_\alpha, \alpha \in \{1,\ldots,N\}\, .$$

Therefore, for $\xi \in \Lambda_\alpha^+$ we may define a *directed and rescaled $(\tfrac{{\mathbb{T}}}{\lambda \sigma})^3 = (\tfrac{{\mathbb{R}}}{2\pi \lambda \sigma {\mathbb{Z}}})^3$-periodic Dirichlet kernel* by

$$\begin{align*}
\eta_{(\xi)}(x,t) = \eta_{\xi,\lambda,\sigma,r,\mu}(x,t) = D_r\left(\lambda \sigma N_{\Lambda} (\xi \cdot x + \mu t), \lambda \sigma N_{\Lambda} A_\xi \cdot x, \lambda \sigma N_{\Lambda} (\xi \times A_\xi)\cdot x\right) \, . \tag{21}\end{align*}$$

For $\xi \in \Lambda_\alpha^-$ we define $\eta_{(\xi)}(x,t) := \eta_{(-\xi)}(x,t)$. The periodicity of $\eta_{(\xi)}$ follows from the fact that $D_r$ is ${\mathbb{T}}^3$-periodic, and the definition of $N_{\Lambda}$. We emphasize that we have the important identity

$$\begin{align*}
\frac{1}{\mu}\partial_t \eta_{(\xi)}(x,t) = \pm (\xi\cdot\nabla)  \eta_{(\xi)}(x,t), \quad \mbox{for all} \quad \xi \in \Lambda_\alpha^{\pm} \tag{22}\end{align*}$$

as a consequence of the fact that the vectors $A_{\xi}$ and $\xi \times A_{\xi}$ are orthogonal to $\xi$.

Note that the map $(x_1,x_2,x_3) \mapsto \left(\lambda \sigma N_{\Lambda} (\xi \cdot x + \mu t), \lambda \sigma N_{\Lambda} A_\xi \cdot x, \lambda \sigma N_{\Lambda} (\xi \times A_\xi)\cdot x\right)$ is the composition of a rotation by a rational orthogonal matrix which maps $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ to $(\xi, A_\xi, \xi \times A_\xi)$, a rescaling by $\lambda \sigma N_{\Lambda}$, and a translation by $\lambda \sigma N_{\Lambda} \mu t e_1$. These are all volume preserving transformations on ${\mathbb{T}}^3$, and thus by our choice of normalization for (19) we have that

$$\begin{align*}
\fint_{{\mathbb{T}}^3} \eta_{(\xi)}^2 (x,t) dx  = 1, \qquad \mbox{and} \qquad \left\|\eta_{(\xi)}\right\|_{L^p({\mathbb{T}}^3)} \lesssim r^{3/2-3/p} \tag{23}\end{align*}$$

for all $1<p\leq \infty$, pointwise in time.

Letting $W_{(\xi)}$ be the Beltrami plane wave at frequency $\lambda$, namely

$$\begin{align*}

W_{(\xi)}(x) = W_{\xi,\lambda}(x) = B_{\xi} e^{i \lambda \xi \cdot x} \, , \tag{24}\end{align*}$$

we have

$$\begin{align*}
{\mathrm{curl\,}}W_{(\xi)} = \lambda W_{(\xi)} \qquad \mbox{and}\qquad {\mathrm{div\,}}W_{(\xi)} = 0\,.
\end{align*}$$

We take $\lambda$ to be a multiple of $N_\Lambda$, so that $W_{(\xi)}$ is ${\mathbb{T}}^3$-periodic. Finally, we define the *intermittent Beltrami wave* ${\mathbb{W}}_{(\xi)}$ as

$$\begin{align*}

{\mathbb{W}}_{(\xi)}(x,t) = {\mathbb{W}}_{\xi,\lambda,\sigma,r,\mu}(x,t) = \eta_{\xi,\lambda,\sigma,r,\mu}(x,t) W_{\xi,\lambda}(x)  = \eta_{(\xi)}(x,t) W_{(\xi)}(x). \tag{25}\end{align*}$$

We first make a few comments concerning the frequency support of ${\mathbb{W}}_{(\xi)}$. In view of (20) and the definition of $\eta_{(\xi)}$, which yields ${\mathbb{P}}_{\leq 2 \lambda \sigma r N_{\Lambda}} \eta_{(\xi)} = \eta_{(\xi)}$, we have that

$$\begin{align*}
{\mathbb{P}}_{\leq 2\lambda } {\mathbb{P}}_{\geq \tfrac{\lambda }{2}} {\mathbb{W}}_{(\xi)} = {\mathbb{W}}_{(\xi)} \, , \tag{26}\end{align*}$$

while for $\xi' \neq -\xi$, by the definition of $c_\Lambda$ in Remark 3.1 we have

$$\begin{align*}
{\mathbb{P}}_{\leq 4\lambda } {\mathbb{P}}_{\geq c_{\Lambda} \lambda } \left({\mathbb{W}}_{(\xi)} \otimes {\mathbb{W}}_{(\xi')}\right) = {\mathbb{W}}_{(\xi)}\otimes {\mathbb{W}}_{(\xi')}. \tag{27}\end{align*}$$

Note that the vector ${\mathbb{W}}_{(\xi)}$ is not anymore divergence free, nor is it an eigenfunction of ${\mathrm{curl\,}}$. These properties only hold to leading order:

$$\begin{align*}
\left\|\frac{1}{\lambda}  {\mathrm{div\,}}{\mathbb{W}}_{(\xi)}\right\|_{L^2} &= \frac{1}{\lambda}\left\|B_{\xi} \cdot \nabla \eta_{(\xi)}\right\|_{L^2} \lesssim\frac{\lambda \sigma r}{\lambda} = \sigma r\\
 \left\|\frac{1}{\lambda} {\mathrm{curl\,}}{\mathbb{W}}_{(\xi)} - {\mathbb{W}}_{(\xi)}\right\|_{L^2} &= \frac{1}{\lambda}\left\|\nabla \eta_{(\xi)} \times B_{\xi}\right\|_{L^2} \lesssim\frac{\lambda \sigma r}{\lambda} = \sigma r
\end{align*}$$

and the parameter $\sigma r$ will be chosen to be small. Moreover, from Propositions 3.1 and 3.1 we have:

*Proof of Proposition 3.2.* The first statement follows from the fact that $\eta_{(-\xi)}(x,t) = \eta_{(\xi)}(x,t)$. Identity (3.2) follows from (3.1) upon noting that $2 {\mathrm{Re\,}}(B_{\xi}\otimes B_{- \xi}) = {\mathrm{Id}}- \xi \otimes \xi$, and the normalization (23). ◻

For the purpose of estimating the oscillation error in Section 5, it is useful to derive a replacement of identity (3.1), in the case of intermittent Beltrami waves. For this purpose, we first recall the vector identity

$$\begin{align*}
(A\cdot \nabla) B+ (B\cdot \nabla) A= \nabla(A\cdot B)-A\times{\mathrm{curl\,}}B-B\times {\mathrm{curl\,}}A.
\end{align*}$$

Hence, for $\xi, \xi' \in \Lambda_\alpha$ we may rewrite

$$\begin{align*}
&{\mathrm{div\,}}\left({\mathbb{W}}_{(\xi)}\otimes {\mathbb{W}}_{(\xi')}+{\mathbb{W}}_{(\xi')}\otimes \mathbb W_{(\xi)}\right)  \\
&\quad =\left(W_{(\xi)}\otimes W_{(\xi')}+W_{(\xi')}\otimes W_{(\xi)}\right)\nabla\left(\eta_{(\xi)}\eta_{(\xi')}\right)
+\eta_{(\xi)}\eta_{(\xi')}\left( (W_{(\xi)}\cdot \nabla) W_{(\xi')}+(W_{(\xi')}\cdot \nabla) W_{(\xi)}\right)  \\
&\quad =\left( (W_{(\xi')}\cdot \nabla) \left(\eta_{(\xi)}\eta_{(\xi')}\right)\right) W_{(\xi)}+\left( (W_{(\xi)}\cdot \nabla) \left(\eta_{(\xi)}\eta_{(\xi')}\right)\right) W_{(\xi')}  \\
&\quad\quad+\eta_{(\xi)}\eta_{(\xi')}\nabla\left(W_{(\xi)}\cdot W_{(\xi')}\right)-\lambda \eta_{(\xi)}\eta_{(\xi')}\left(W_{(\xi)}\times W_{(\xi')}+W_{(\xi')}\times W_{(\xi)}\right)  \\
&\quad =\left( (W_{(\xi')}\cdot \nabla) \left(\eta_{(\xi)}\eta_{(\xi')}\right)\right) W_{(\xi)}+\left( (W_{(\xi)}\cdot \nabla)\left(\eta_{(\xi)}\eta_{(\xi')}\right)\right) W_{(\xi')}+\eta_{(\xi)}\eta_{(\xi')}\nabla\left(W_{(\xi)}\cdot W_{(\xi')}\right) . \tag{28}\end{align*}$$

In the last equality we have used that the cross-product is antisymmetric.

Let us now restrict to the case $\xi+\xi'=0$. Recall that $W_{(\xi)}= \frac{1}{\sqrt 2} (A_{\xi}+i\xi\times A_{\xi})e^{i\lambda \xi\cdot x}$ , $\xi\cdot A_\xi = 0$, and $|A_{\xi}|=1$. Therefore, when $\xi' = -\xi$ the last term on the right side of (28) is zero, as $W_{(\xi)}\cdot W_{(-\xi)} = 1$. Thus we obtain

$$\begin{align*}
{\mathrm{div\,}}\left({\mathbb{W}}_{(\xi)}\otimes {\mathbb{W}}_{(-\xi)}+{\mathbb{W}}_{(-\xi)}\otimes {\mathbb{W}}_{(\xi)}\right)
&=
\left( (W_{(-\xi)}\cdot \nabla) \eta_{(\xi)}^2\right)W_{(\xi)}+\left( (W_{(\xi)}\cdot \nabla) \eta_{(\xi)}^2\right)W_{(-\xi)}
\notag \\
&=\left( (A_{\xi}\cdot \nabla) \eta_{(\xi)}^2\right) A_{\xi}+\left( ( (\xi\times A_{\xi})\cdot \nabla) \eta_{\xi}^2\right)(\xi\times A_{\xi})
\notag \\
&=\nabla \eta_{(\xi)}^2- \left( (\xi\cdot \nabla) \eta_{(\xi)}^2\right)\xi
\, .
\end{align*}$$

In the last equality above we have used that $\left\{ \xi, A_\xi, \xi\times A_\xi\right\}$ is an orthonormal basis of ${\mathbb{R}}^3$. The above identity and property (22) of $\eta_{(\xi)}$ shows that

$$\begin{align*}
{\mathrm{div\,}}\left({\mathbb{W}}_{(\xi)}\otimes {\mathbb{W}}_{(-\xi)}+{\mathbb{W}}_{(-\xi)}\otimes {\mathbb{W}}_{(\xi)}\right) = \nabla \eta_{(\xi)}^2 - \frac{\xi}{\mu} \partial_t \eta_{(\xi)}^2. \tag{29}\end{align*}$$

which is the key identity that motivates the introduction of temporal oscillations in the problem.

Recall, the intermittent Beltrami waves were designed to include additional oscillations that cancel in order to minimize their $L^1$ norm, in a way that is analogous to the cancellations of the Dirichlet kernel. In this direction, an immediate consequence of property (23) of $\eta_{(\xi)}$, of the frequency localization in the spatial variable (26), and of the frequency of the temporal oscillations, are the following bounds for $\eta_{(\xi)}$ and the the intermittent Beltrami waves ${\mathbb{W}}_{(\xi)}$:

## 3.3 $L^p$ decorrelation

We now introduce a crucial lemma from (BMV17) that will be used throughout the paper. Suppose we wish to estimate

$$\left\|f \; \mathbb W_{(\xi)}\right\|_{L^1}$$

for some arbitrary function $f:\mathbb T^3\rightarrow \mathbb R$. The trivial estimate is

$$\begin{align*}

\left\|f \; \mathbb W_{(\xi)}\right\|_{L^1}\lesssim \left\|f\right\|_{L^2}\left\|\mathbb W_{(\xi)}\right\|_{L^2}\,.
\end{align*}$$

Such an estimate does not however take advantage of the special structure of the $(2\pi\lambda \sigma)^{-1}$ periodic function $\mathbb W_{(\xi)} e^{-i \lambda \xi \cdot x}$. It turns out that if say $f$ has frequency contained in a ball of radius $\mu$ and $\lambda\sigma\gg \mu$ then one obtains the improved estimate

$$\begin{align*}

\left\|f \; \mathbb W_{(\xi)}\right\|_{L^1}\lesssim \left\|f\right\|_{L^1}\left\|\mathbb W_{(\xi)}\right\|_{L^1}
\end{align*}$$

which gives us the needed gain because $\left\|\mathbb W_{(\xi)}\right\|_{L^1} \ll \left\|\mathbb W_{(\xi)}\right\|_{L^2}$. This idea is one of the key insights of (BMV17) and is summarized in Lemma 3.3 below. For convenience we include the proof in Appendix A.

# 4 The perturbation

In this section we will construct the perturbation $w_{q+1}$.

## 4.1 Mollification of $v_q$

In order to avoid a loss of derivative, we replace $v_q$ by a mollified velocity field $v_\ell$. Let $\{ \phi_{\varepsilon} \}_{\varepsilon>0}$ be a family of standard Friedrichs mollifiers (of compact support of radius $2$) on ${\mathbb{R}}^3$ (space), and $\{\varphi_{\varepsilon}\}_{\varepsilon>0}$ be a family of standard Friedrichs mollifiers (of compact support of width $2$) on ${\mathbb{R}}$ (time). We define a mollification of $v_q$ and $\mathring R_q$ in space and time, at length scale and time scale $\ell$ (which is defined in (46) below) by

$$\begin{align*}
v_{\ell} = (v_q \ast_x \phi_{\ell}) \ast_t \varphi_{\ell}  \, ,\\
\mathring R_{\ell} = (\mathring R_q \ast_x \phi_{\ell}) \ast_t \varphi_{\ell} \,. \tag{30}\end{align*}$$

Then using (2) we obtain that $(v_\ell,\mathring R_\ell)$ obey

$$\begin{align*}
\partial_t  v_\ell + {\mathrm{div\,}}(v_\ell \otimes v_\ell) + \nabla p_\ell - \Delta v_\ell 
&= {\mathrm{div\,}}\Big(  \mathring R_\ell + \widetilde R_{\rm commutator} \Big)\, , \tag{31}\\
{\mathrm{div\,}}v_\ell &= 0 \, , \tag{32}\end{align*}$$

where the new pressure $p_\ell$ and the traceless symmetric commutator stress $\widetilde R_{\rm commutator}$ are given by

$$\begin{align*}
\widetilde p_\ell &= (p_q \ast_x \phi_{\ell}) \ast_t \varphi_{\ell} - \left(|v_\ell|^2  - (|v_q|^2 \ast_x \phi_\ell) \ast_t \varphi_\ell \right)  \, , \\
\widetilde R_{\rm commutator} &= (v_\ell \mathring \otimes v_\ell) - ((v_q \mathring \otimes v_q)\ast_x \phi_{\ell}) \ast_t \varphi_{\ell} \, . \tag{33}\end{align*}$$

Here we have used $a \mathring \otimes b$ to denote the traceless part of the tensor $a \otimes b$.

Note that in view of (6) the commutator stress $\widetilde R_{\rm commutator}$ obeys the lossy estimate

$$\begin{align*}
\left\| \widetilde R_{\rm commutator}\right\|_{L^\infty} \lesssim\ell \left\|v_q\otimes v_q\right\|_{C^{1}}\lesssim\ell \left\|v_q\right\|_{C^{1}}\left\|v_q\right\|_{L^{\infty}}\lesssim\ell \lambda_q^8. \tag{34}\end{align*}$$

The parameter $\ell$ will be chosen (cf. (46) below) to satisfy

$$\begin{align*}
(\sigma \lambda_{q+1})^{-\tfrac 12} \ll \ell \ll  \lambda_q^{-19} \delta_{q+1} 
  \,. \tag{35}\end{align*}$$

In particular, $\mathring R_\ell$ inherits the $L^1$ bound of $\mathring R_q$ from (7), and in view (8) and the upper bound on $\ell$ in (35), we have that

$$\begin{align*}
\left\|\mathring R_\ell\right\|_{C^N_{t,x}} \lesssim\lambda_q^{10}\ell^{-N+1}\lesssim\ell^{-N}\,. \tag{36}\end{align*}$$

Moreover, from (6) and the upper bound on $\ell$ from (35) we obtain the bounds

$$\begin{align*}
 \left\|v_q - v_\ell\right\|_{L^\infty}& \lesssim\ell\left\|v_q\right\|_{C^1}\lesssim\ell \lambda_q^4 
  \, , \tag{37}\\
  \left\|v_\ell\right\|_{C^N_{x,t}}& \lesssim\ell^{1-N}\left\|v_q\right\|_{C^1}\lesssim\ell^{1-N}\lambda_q^4\lesssim\ell^{-N}\, . \tag{38}\end{align*}$$

## 4.2 Stress cutoffs

Because the Reynolds stress $\mathring R_\ell$ is not spatially homogenous, we introduce stress cutoff functions. We let $0 \leq \widetilde\chi_0, \widetilde\chi \leq 1$ be bump functions adapted to the intervals $[0,4]$ and $[1/4,4]$ respectively, such that together they form a partition of unity:

$$\begin{align*}
\widetilde\chi_{0}^2(y) + \sum_{i\geq 1}  \widetilde\chi^2_{i}(y) \equiv 1, \quad \mbox{where} \quad \widetilde\chi_i (y) = \widetilde\chi(4^{-i} y), \tag{39}\end{align*}$$

for any $y>0$. We then define

$$\begin{align*}
\chi_{(i)}(x,t)=\chi_{i,q+1}(x,t) = \widetilde\chi_{i}\left( \left\langle \frac{\mathring R_{\ell}(x,t)}{100 \lambda_q^{-\varepsilon_R}\delta_{q+1}}\right\rangle\right) \tag{40}\end{align*}$$

for all $i\geq 0$. Here and throughout the paper we use the notation $\langle A \rangle = (1+ |A|^2)^{1/2}$ where $|A|$ denotes the Euclidean norm of the matrix $A$. By definition the cutoffs $\chi_{(i)}$ form a partition of unity

$$\begin{align*}
\sum_{i\geq 0} \chi_{(i)}^2 \equiv 1 \tag{41}\end{align*}$$

and we will show in Lemma 4.5 below that there exists an index $i_{\rm max} = i_{\rm max}(q)$, such that $\chi_{(i)} \equiv 0$ for all $i > i_{\rm max}$, and moreover that $4^{i_{\rm max}} \lesssim\ell^{-1}$.

## 4.3 The definition of the velocity increment

Define the coefficient function $a_{\xi,i,q+1}$ by

$$a_{(\xi)}:= a_{\xi,i,q+1}:=\rho_i^{\tfrac 12} \chi_{i,q+1} \gamma_{(\xi)}\left({\mathrm{Id}}- \frac{\mathring R_{\ell}}{ \rho_i(t)}\right). \tag{42}$$

where for $i\geq 1$, the parameters $\rho_i$ are defined by

$$\begin{align*}

\rho_i:= \lambda_q^{-\varepsilon_R} \delta_{q+1} 4^{i+c_0} \tag{43}\end{align*}$$

where $c_0 \in {\mathbb{N}}$ is a sufficiently large constant, which depends on the $\varepsilon_\gamma$ in Proposition 3.2. The addition of the factor $4^{c_0}$ ensures that the argument of $\gamma_{(\xi)}$ is in the range of definition. The definition $\rho_0$ is slightly more complicated and as such its definition will be delayed to Section 4.4 below, see (55) and (56). Modulo the definition of $\rho_0$, we note that as a consequence of (27), (3.2), (41), and (42) we have

$$\begin{align*}
\sum_{i\geq 0}\sum_{\xi,\xi' \in \Lambda_{(i)}}a_{(\xi)}^2\fint_{\mathbb T^3}\left(\mathbb W_{(\xi)}\otimes \mathbb W_{(\xi')} \right)dx=
\sum_{i\geq 0} \rho_i \chi_{(i)}^2{\mathrm{Id}}-\mathring R_{\ell}\,, \tag{44}\end{align*}$$

which justifies the definition of the amplitude functions $a_{(\xi)}$.

By a slight abuse of notation, let us now fix $\lambda, \sigma, r$, and $\mu$ for the short hand notation $\mathbb  W_{(\xi)}$, $W_{(\xi)}$ and $\eta_{(\xi)}$ introduced in Section 3.2 (cf. (21), (24), (25)):

$$\mathbb  W_{(\xi)}:=\mathbb W_{\xi,\lambda_{q+1},\sigma ,r ,\mu},\quad W_{(\xi)}:=W_{\xi,\lambda_{q+1}} \quad \mbox{and}\quad \eta_{(\xi)}:=\eta_{\xi,\lambda_{q+1},\sigma ,r ,\mu}\, ,$$

where the integer $r$, the parameter $\sigma$, and the parameter $\mu$ are defined by

$$\begin{align*}
r = \lambda_{q+1}^{\tfrac 34}, \qquad \sigma = \lambda_{q+1}^{-\tfrac {15}{16}}\qquad \mbox{and} \qquad \mu=\lambda_{q+1}^{\tfrac 54}\,. \tag{45}\end{align*}$$

The fact that $\lambda_{q+1} \sigma \in {\mathbb{N}}$ is ensured by our choices $a\in {\mathbb{N}}$ and $b \in 16 {\mathbb{N}}$. In order to ensure $\lambda_{q+1}$ is a multiple of $N_{\Lambda}$, we need to choose $a$ which is a multiple of $N_{\Lambda}$. Moreover, at this stage we fix

$$\begin{align*}
\ell = \lambda_q^{-20} \, , \tag{46}\end{align*}$$

which in view of the choice of $\sigma$ in (45), ensures that (35) holds, upon taking $\lambda_0$ sufficiently large. In view of (46), throughout the rest of the paper we may use either $\ell^{\varepsilon} \leq \lambda_0^{-20 \varepsilon}$ or $\lambda_{q}^{-\varepsilon} \leq \lambda_0^{-\varepsilon}$, with $\varepsilon>0$ arbitrarily small, to absorb any of the constants (which are $q$-independent) appearing due to $\lesssim$ signs in the below inequalities. This is possible by choosing $\lambda_0 =  a$, sufficiently large.

The *principal part of $w_{q+1}$* is defined as

$$w^{(p)}_{q+1}:=\sum_{i}\sum_{\xi\in \Lambda_{(i)}}a_{(\xi)} \; \mathbb  W_{(\xi)}\,, \tag{47}$$

where the sum is over $0 \leq i \leq i_{\rm max}(q)$. The sets $\Lambda_{(i)}$ are defined as follows. In Lemma 3.1 it suffices to take $N=2$, so that $\alpha \in \{ \alpha_0, \alpha_1 \}$, and we define $\Lambda_{(i)} = \Lambda_{\alpha_{i {\rm \, mod\, } 2}}$. This choice is allowable since $\chi_i \chi_{j} \equiv 0$ for $\left|i-j\right|\geq 2$. In order to fix the fact that $w_{q+1}^{(p)}$ is not divergence free, we define an *incompressibility corrector* by

$$\begin{align*}
w^{(c)}_{q+1}:=&\frac{1}{\lambda_{q+1}}\sum_{i}\sum_{\xi\in \Lambda_{(i)}}\nabla \left(a_{(\xi)}\eta_{(\xi)} \right)\times W_{(\xi)}\,. \tag{48}\end{align*}$$

Using that ${\mathrm{div\,}}W_{(\xi)} = 0$, we then have

$$\begin{align*}

w_{q+1}^{(p)}+w_{q+1}^{(c)}=\frac{ {1} }{\lambda_{q+1}}\sum_{i}\sum_{\xi\in \Lambda_{(i)}}{\mathrm{curl\,}}\left(a_{(\xi)}\eta_{(\xi)} W_{(\xi)}\right)=\frac{ {1} }{\lambda_{q+1}}{\mathrm{curl\,}}(w_{q+1}^{(p)})\,, \tag{49}\end{align*}$$

and thus

$${\mathrm{div\,}}\left(w_{q+1}^{(p)}+w_{q+1}^{(c)}\right)=0\,.$$

In addition to the incompressibility corrector $w_{q+1}^{(c)}$, we introduce a *temporal corrector* $w_{q+1}^{(t)}$, which is defined by

$$w^{(t)}_{q+1}:=\frac{1}{\mu}\sum_{i}\sum_{\xi\in \Lambda_{(i)}^+}\mathbb P_{H}\mathbb P_{\neq 0}\left(a_{(\xi)}^2\eta_{(\xi)}^2 \xi\right)\,. \tag{50}$$

Here we have denoted by ${\mathbb{P}}_{\neq 0}$ the operator which projects a function onto its nonzero frequencies ${\mathbb{P}}_{\neq 0} f = f - \fint_{{\mathbb{T}}^3} f$, and have used $\mathbb P_{H}$ for the usual Helmholtz (or Leray) projector onto divergence-free vector fields, ${\mathbb{P}}_H f  = f  - \nabla (\Delta^{-1} {\mathrm{div\,}}f)$. The purpose of the corrector $w_{q+1}^{(t)}$ becomes apparent upon recalling (29). Indeed, if we multiply identity (29) by $a_{(\xi)}^2$, remove the mean and a suitable pressure gradient, the leading order term left is $-(\tfrac{1}{\mu}) {\mathbb{P}}_{H} {\mathbb{P}}_{\neq 0} ( \xi a_{(\xi)}^2 \partial_t \eta_{(\xi)}^2)$, see (70) below. This term is not of high frequency (proportional to $\lambda_{q+1}$). Moreover, upon writing this term as the divergence of a symmetric stress, the size of this stress term in $L^1$ is $\delta_{q+1}$, instead of $\delta_{q+2}$; thus this term does not obey a favorable estimate and has to be cancelled altogether. The corrector $w_{q+1}^{(t)}$ is designed such that its *time derivative* achieves precisely this goal, of cancelling the $-(\tfrac{1}{\mu}) {\mathbb{P}}_{H} {\mathbb{P}}_{\neq 0} ( \xi a_{(\xi)}^2 \partial_t \eta_{(\xi)}^2)$ term.

Finally, we define the velocity increment $w_{q+1}$ by

$$w_{q+1}:=w_{q+1}^{(p)}+w_{q+1}^{(c)}+w_{q+1}^{(t)}, \tag{51}$$

which is by construction mean zero and divergence-free. The new velocity field $v_{q+1}$ is then defined as

$$v_{q+1} = v_\ell + w_{q+1} \, . \tag{52}$$

## 4.4 The definition of $\rho_0$

It follows from (44) that with the $\rho_i$ defined above we have

$$\begin{align*}
\sum_{i\geq 1}\int_{\mathbb T^3}\left|\sum_{\xi\in \Lambda_{(i)}} a_{(\xi)}\mathbb W_{(\xi)}\right|^2\,dx
&=\sum_{i\geq 1} \sum_{\xi,   \xi' \in \Lambda_{(i)}} \int_{\mathbb T^3} a_{(\xi)}a_{(\xi')} {\mathrm{tr\,}}(\mathbb W_{(\xi)} \otimes \mathbb W_{(-\xi')} )\,dx
\\
&=\sum_{i\geq 1} \sum_{\xi \in \Lambda_{(i)}} \int_{\mathbb T^3}  a^2_{(\xi)}   {\mathrm{tr\,}}\fint_{\mathbb T^3}(\mathbb W_{(\xi)} \otimes \mathbb W_{(-\xi)} )\,dx + \mbox{error}
\\
&= 3 \sum_{i\geq 1}\rho_i\int_{\mathbb T^3}\chi_{(i)}^2\, dx  + \mbox{error}\, , \tag{53}\end{align*}$$

where the error term can be made arbitrarily small since the spatial frequency of the $a_{(\xi)}$’s is $\ell^{-1}$, while the minimal separation of frequencies of $\mathbb W_{(\xi)} \otimes \mathbb W_{-(\xi')}$ is $\lambda_{q+1}\sigma \gg \ell^{-1}$. The term labeled as *error* on the right side of (53) above will be estimated precisely in Section 6 below. We will show in the next section, Lemma 4.5 that

$$\begin{align*}

\sum_{i\geq 1}\rho_i\int_{\mathbb T^3}\chi_{(i)}^2\, dx \lesssim \delta_{q+1}\lambda_{q}^{-\varepsilon_R}\,. \tag{54}\end{align*}$$

In order to ensure (9) is satisfied for $q+1$, we design $\rho_0$ such that

$$\begin{align*}

\int_{\mathbb T^3}\left|\sum_{\xi\in \Lambda_{(0)}} a_{(\xi)}\mathbb W_{(\xi)}\right|^2\,dx
\approx \widetilde e(t):=e(t)-\int_{\mathbb T^3}\left|v_q\right|^2\,dx - 3\sum_{i\geq 1}\rho_i\int_{\mathbb T^3}\chi_{i}^2\, dx\,.
\end{align*}$$

We thus define the auxiliary function

$$\begin{align*}
 
\rho(t):=\frac{1}{3 \left|\mathbb T^3\right|}\left(\int_{\mathbb T^3} \chi_0^2\,dx\right)^{-1}\max\left(\widetilde e(t)-\frac{\delta_{q+2}}{2},\,0\right)\,. \tag{55}\end{align*}$$

The term $-\tfrac{\delta_{q+2}}{2}$ is added to ensure that we leave room for future corrections and the $\max$ is in place to ensure that we do not correct the energy when the energy of $v_q$ is already sufficiently close to the prescribed energy profile. This later property will allow us to take energy profiles with compact support. Finally, in order to ensure $\rho_0^{\tfrac 12}$ is sufficiently smooth, we define $\rho_0$ as the square of the mollification of $\rho^{\tfrac 12}$ at time scale $\ell$

$$\begin{align*}

\rho_0= \left( (\rho^{\tfrac 12})  \ast_t \varphi_{\ell} \right)^2\,. \tag{56}\end{align*}$$

We note that (9) and (4.5) below imply that

$$\left\|\rho_0\right\|_{C^0_t} \leq 2\delta_{q+1} \quad\mbox{and}\quad \left\|\rho_0^{\tfrac 12}\right\|_{C^{N}_{t}}\lesssim\delta_{q+1}^{\tfrac 12}\ell^{-N} \tag{57}$$

for $N \geq 1$. By a slight abuse of notation we will denote

$$\begin{align*}

\frac{\mathring R_{\ell}}{ \rho_0(t)}=\begin{cases}\frac{\mathring R_{\ell}}{ \rho_0(t)}&\mbox{if }  \chi_0\neq 0\mbox{ and }\mathring R_{\ell}\neq 0 \, ,\\
0&\mbox{otherwise}\,.
\end{cases} \tag{58}\end{align*}$$

Observe that if $\chi_0\neq 0$ and $\mathring R_{\ell}\neq 0$, then (10) and (54) ensure that $\rho_0>0$. In order to ensure that ${\mathrm{Id}}- \frac{\mathring R_{\ell}}{ \rho_0(t)}$ is in the domain of the functions $\gamma_{(\xi)}$ from Proposition 3.2, we will need to ensure that

$$\begin{align*}

\left\|\frac{\mathring R_{\ell}}{ \rho_0(t)}\right\|_{L^{\infty}({\mathrm{supp\,}}\chi_{(0)})}\leq \varepsilon_{\gamma} \, . \tag{59}\end{align*}$$

We give the proof of (59) next. Owing to the estimate

$$\begin{align*}

\left|e(t)-\int_{\mathbb T^3}\left|v_q(x,t)\right|^2 \, dx-e(t')-\int_{\mathbb T^3}\left|v_q(x,t')\right|^2\right| \, dx \lesssim\ell^{\tfrac12}
\end{align*}$$

for $t'\in(t-\ell,t+\ell)$ which follows from Lemma 6 in Section 6, and the inequality $\ell^{\tfrac 12} \ll \delta_{q+1}$, we may apply (10) to conclude that it is sufficient to check the above condition when

$$\begin{align*}

e(t)-\int_{\mathbb T^3}\left|v_q(x,t)\right|^2\,dx \geq \frac{\delta_{q+1}}{200}\,.
\end{align*}$$

Then by (54), the above lower bound implies

$$\begin{align*}

\widetilde e(t) \geq \frac{\delta_{q+1}}{400}\,.
\end{align*}$$

and thus

$$\begin{align*}

\rho(t)\geq \frac{1}{\left|\mathbb T^3\right|}\left(\frac{\delta_{q+1}}{400}-\frac{\delta_{q+2}}{2}\right)\geq\frac{\delta_{q+1}}{500}
\end{align*}$$

where we used (4.5) from Lemma 4.5 below to bound the integral. Finally, using the estimate (6) from Section 6 we obtain

$$\begin{equation*}
\rho_0(t) \geq \frac{\delta_{q+1}}{600} \, .
\end{equation*}$$

Since on the support of $\chi_0$ we have $\left|\mathring R_{\ell}\right|\leq 1000 \lambda_{q}^{-\varepsilon_R}\delta_{q+1}$ we obtain (59).

## 4.5 Estimates of the perturbation

We first collect a number of estimates concerning the cutoffs $\chi_{(i)}$ defined in (40).

*Proof of Lemma 4.5.* Let $i \geq 1$. By the definition of $\widetilde\chi_{i}$ we have that $\chi_{(i)} = 0$ for all $(x,t)$ such that

$$\langle 100^{-1}\lambda_q^{\varepsilon_R} \delta_{q+1}^{-1} \mathring R_{\ell}(x,t)\rangle < 4^{i-1} \, .$$

Using the inductive assumption (8), we have that

$$\left\|\mathring R_\ell\right\|_{L^\infty} \lesssim\left\|\mathring R_\ell\right\|_{C^1} \lesssim\left\|\mathring R_q\right\|_{C^1} \leq C_{\rm max} \lambda_{q}^{10} \leq \lambda_{q}^{10 +\varepsilon_R}$$

since the implicit constant $C_{\rm max}$ is independent of $q$ and of $\varepsilon_R$ (it only depends on norms of the mollifier $\phi$ used to define $\mathring R_{\ell}$), and thus we have $C_{\rm max} \leq \lambda_q^{\varepsilon_R}$. Therefore, if $i\geq 1$ is large enough such that

$$\langle 100^{-1}  \delta_{q+1}^{-1}  \lambda_{q}^{10 +2 \varepsilon_R} \rangle \leq 4^{i-2} \,,$$

Next we turn to the errors involving correctors, for which we appeal to $L^p$ interpolation, the Poincaré inequality, and Proposition 4.5:

$$\begin{align*}
\left\| \widetilde R_{\rm corrector}\right\|_{L^p} 
&\leq \left\|\mathcal R {\mathrm{div\,}}\left((w_{q+1}^{(c)}+w_{q+1}^{(t)}) \otimes w_{q+1}+ w_{q+1}^{(p)} \otimes (w_{q+1}^{(c)}+w_{q+1}^{(t)}) \right)\right\|_{L^p}\\
&\lesssim   \left\|(w_{q+1}^{(c)}+w_{q+1}^{(t)}) \otimes w_{q+1}\right\|_{L^1}^{\tfrac{1}{p}}   \left\|(w_{q+1}^{(c)}+w_{q+1}^{(t)}) \otimes w_{q+1}\right\|_{L^\infty}^{1-\tfrac 1p}\\
&\quad+ \left\|w_{q+1}^{(p)} \otimes (w_{q+1}^{(c)}+w_{q+1}^{(t)})\right\|_{L^1}^{\tfrac 1p}   \left\|w_{q+1}^{(p)} \otimes (w_{q+1}^{(c)}+w_{q+1}^{(t)})\right\|_{L^\infty}^{1-\tfrac1p}
\\
&\lesssim (r^{\tfrac 32}\ell^{-1}\mu^{-1})^{\tfrac1p} \delta_{q+1}^{\tfrac1p} \lambda_{q+1}^{3(1-\tfrac1p)}
\\
&\lesssim (r^{\tfrac 32}\ell^{-1}\mu^{-1})^{\tfrac1p} \lambda_{q+1}^{3(1-\tfrac 1p)}\,.
\end{align*}$$

Due to (65) this estimate is sufficient.

## 5.3 Oscillation error

In this section we estimate the remaining error, $\widetilde R_{\rm oscillation}$ which obeys

$$\begin{align*}
&{\mathrm{div\,}}\left( \widetilde R_{\rm oscillation} \right) + \nabla P ={\mathrm{div\,}}\left(w^{(p)}_{q+1}\otimes w^{(p)}_{q+1} + \mathring R_{\ell}\right)+\partial_t w^{(t)}_{q+1}  \,, \tag{67}\end{align*}$$

where the pressure term $P$ is given by

$$\begin{align*}
P =   \sum_{i\geq 0} \rho_i \chi_{(i)}^2  + \frac 12 \sum_{i,j}\sum_{\xi\in \Lambda_{(i)},\xi'\in \Lambda_{(j)}} a_{(\xi)}a_{(\xi')} {\mathbb{P}}_{\neq 0} \left({\mathbb{W}}_{(\xi)} \cdot {\mathbb{W}}_{(\xi')} \right) - \sum_{i}\sum_{\xi\in \Lambda_{(i)}^+} \frac{1}{\mu} \Delta^{-1} {\mathrm{div\,}}\partial_t  \left(a_{(\xi)}^2  \eta_{(\xi)}^2 \xi\right)
\, . \tag{68}\end{align*}$$

Recall from the definition of $w_{q+1}^{(p)}$ and of the coefficients $a_{(\xi)}$, via (44) we have

$$\begin{align*}
&{\mathrm{div\,}}\left(w^{(p)}_{q+1}\otimes w^{(p)}_{q+1} \right) +   {\mathrm{div\,}}{\mathring R_{\ell}}  \\
&\qquad = \sum_{i,j}\sum_{\xi\in \Lambda_{(i)},\xi'\in \Lambda_{(j)}}{\mathrm{div\,}}\left(a_{(\xi)}a_{(\xi')}\mathbb W_{(\xi)}\otimes \mathbb W_{(\xi')}\right)+ {\mathrm{div\,}}\mathring R_{\ell} 
 \\
&\qquad = \sum_{i,j}\sum_{\xi\in \Lambda_{(i)},\xi'\in \Lambda_{(j)}}{\mathrm{div\,}}\left(a_{(\xi)}a_{(\xi')}\left(\mathbb W_{(\xi)}\otimes \mathbb W_{(\xi')}-\fint_{{\mathbb{T}}^3} \mathbb W_{(\xi)}\otimes \mathbb W_{(\xi')} \, dx \right)\right)  +\nabla \left( \sum_{i\geq 0} \rho_i \chi_{(i)}^2  \right)
 \\
&\qquad =\sum_{i,j}\sum_{\xi\in \Lambda_{(i)},\xi'\in \Lambda_{(j)}}\underbrace{{\mathrm{div\,}}\left(a_{(\xi)}a_{(\xi')}\mathbb P_{{\geq} \tfrac{\lambda_{q+1}\sigma}{2}}\left(\mathbb W_{(\xi)}\otimes \mathbb W_{(\xi')} \right)\right)}_{E_{(\xi,\xi')}} \; +\; \nabla \left( \sum_{i\geq 0} \rho_i \chi_{(i)}^2  \right) \, . \tag{69}\end{align*}$$

Here we use that the minimal separation between active frequencies of ${\mathbb W}_{(\xi)} \otimes {\mathbb W}_{(\xi')}$ and the $0$ frequency is given by $\lambda_{q+1} \sigma$ for $\xi' = - \xi$, and by $c_\Lambda \lambda_{q+1}\geq \lambda_{q+1} \sigma$ for $\xi' \neq -\xi$. We proceed to estimate each symmetrized summand $E_{(\xi,\xi')}+E_{(\xi',\xi)}$ individually. We split

$$\begin{align*}
E_{(\xi,\xi')}+E_{(\xi',\xi)}&=  \mathbb P_{\neq 0}\left(\mathbb P_{{\geq}\tfrac{\lambda_{q+1}\sigma}{2}}\left(\mathbb W_{(\xi)}\otimes \mathbb W_{(\xi')}+\mathbb W_{(\xi')}\otimes \mathbb W_{(\xi)}\right)\nabla \left( a_{(\xi)}a_{(\xi')}\right) \right)\\
&\quad + \mathbb P_{\neq 0}\left(a_{(\xi)}a_{(\xi')}{\mathrm{div\,}}\left(\mathbb W_{(\xi)}\otimes \mathbb W_{(\xi')}+\mathbb W_{(\xi')}\otimes \mathbb W_{(\xi)}\right) \right)\notag\\
&=: E_{(\xi,\xi',1)}+E_{(\xi,\xi',2)} \, .\notag
\end{align*}$$

Here we used the fact that $E_{(\xi,\xi')}+E_{(\xi,\xi')}$ has zero mean to subtract the mean from each of the the two terms on the right hand side of the above. We have also removed the unnecessary frequency projection $P_{{\geq} \tfrac{\lambda_{q+1}\sigma}{2}}$ from the second term.

The term $E_{(\xi,\xi',1)}$ can easily be estimated using Lemma 4.5 and Lemma B, estimate (B), with $\lambda = \ell^{-1}$, $C_a = \ell^{-2}$, $\kappa = \tfrac{\lambda_{q+1} \sigma}{2}$, and $L$ sufficiently large, as

$$\begin{align*}
\left\|\mathcal R E_{(\xi,\xi',1)}\right\|_{L^p}&\lesssim\left\|\left|\nabla\right|^{-1}  E_{(\xi,\xi',1)}\right\|_{L^p}
 \\
& \lesssim\left\|\left|\nabla\right|^{-1}{\mathbb{P}}_{\neq 0} \left( \mathbb P_{{\geq} \tfrac{\lambda_{q+1}\sigma}{2}}\left(\mathbb W_{(\xi)}\otimes \mathbb W_{(\xi')}\right) \nabla \left( a_{(\xi)}a_{(\xi')}\right)  \right)\right\|_{L^p}
 \\
&\lesssim\frac{1}{\ell^{2}\lambda_{q+1}\sigma}\left(1+\frac{1}{\ell^L\left(\lambda_{q+1} \sigma\right)^{L-2}}\right)  \left\|\mathbb W_{(\xi)}\otimes \mathbb W_{(\xi')}\right\|_{L^p} \\
&\lesssim\frac{1}{\ell^{2}\lambda_{q+1}\sigma}  \left\|\mathbb W_{(\xi)}\right\|_{L^{2p}} \left\|\mathbb W_{(\xi')}\right\|_{L^{2p}} \\
&\lesssim\frac{ r^{3-\tfrac {3}{p}}}{\ell^{2}\lambda_{q+1}\sigma} \, .
\end{align*}$$

In the last inequality above we have used estimate (3.2), and in the second to last inequality we have used that for $b$ sufficiently large and $L$ sufficiently large we have $\ell^{-L} (\lambda_{q+1} \sigma)^{2-L} \lesssim 1$. Indeed, this inequality holds under the conditions $L\geq 3$ and $\tfrac{b(L-2)}{16} \geq 20 L$. After summing in $i$ and $\xi$ we incur an additional loss of $\ell^{-1}$. By (65) this bound is consistent with (5).

For the term $E_{(\xi,\xi',2)}$, we split into two cases: $\xi+\xi'\neq 0$ and $\xi+\xi'=0$. Let us first consider the case $\xi+\xi'\neq 0$. Applying the identity (28), and using (27) we have

$$\begin{align*}
&a_{(\xi)}a_{(\xi')}{\mathrm{div\,}}\left( \mathbb  W_{(\xi)}\otimes \mathbb W_{( \xi')} + \mathbb  W_{(\xi')}\otimes \mathbb W_{( \xi)}\right)\notag\\
&\quad=a_{(\xi)}a_{(\xi')}\left(\left(W_{(\xi')}\cdot \nabla\left(\eta_{(\xi)}\eta_{(\xi')}\right)\right) W_{(\xi)}+\left(W_{(\xi)}\cdot \nabla\left(\eta_{(\xi)}\eta_{(\xi')}\right)\right) W_{(\xi')}\right)\notag\\
&\quad\quad+a_{(\xi)}a_{(\xi')}\eta_{(\xi)}\eta_{(\xi')}\nabla\left(W_{(\xi)}\cdot W_{(\xi')}\right)\notag\\
&\quad=a_{(\xi)}a_{(\xi')}\mathbb P_{\geq  c_{\Lambda}\lambda_{q+1}}\left(\nabla\left(\eta_{(\xi)}\eta_{(\xi')}\right)\left(W_{(\xi')} \otimes W_{(\xi)}+W_{(\xi)} \otimes W_{(\xi')}\right)\right)\notag\\
&\quad\quad+\nabla\left(a_{(\xi)}a_{(\xi')}\mathbb W_{(\xi)}\cdot\mathbb W_{(\xi')}\right)-\nabla \left(a_{(\xi)}a_{(\xi')}\right) \mathbb P_{\geq  c_{\Lambda} \lambda_{q+1}}\left(\mathbb W_{(\xi)}\cdot \mathbb W_{(\xi')}\right)\\
&\quad\quad-a_{(\xi)}a_{(\xi')}\mathbb P_{\geq  c_{\Lambda} \lambda_{q+1}}\left((W_{(\xi)}\cdot W_{(\xi')})\nabla (\eta_{(\xi)}\eta_{(\xi')})\right) \, .
\end{align*}$$

The second term is a pressure and to the remaining terms we apply the inverse divergence operator $\mathcal R$. We estimate $\mathcal R$ applied to the third term analogously to $E_{(\xi,\xi',1)}$, and $\mathcal R$ applied to the fourth term can be estimated similarly to the first term. Thus it suffices to estimate $\mathcal R$ applied to the first term. Applying (3.2), Lemma 4.5, estimate (B) of Lemma B, with $\lambda = \ell^{-1}$, $C_a = \ell^{-2}$, $\kappa =c_{\Lambda}\lambda_{q+1}$, and for $b$ and $L$ sufficiently large ($L\geq 3$ and $b(L-2) \geq 20 L$ suffices), we obtain

$$\begin{align*}
&\left\|\mathcal R \left(a_{(\xi)}a_{(\xi')}\mathbb P_{\geq c_{\Lambda}\lambda_{q+1}}\left(\nabla\left(\eta_{(\xi)}\eta_{(\xi')}\right)(W_{(\xi')} \otimes W_{(\xi)}+W_{(\xi)} \otimes W_{(\xi')})\right)\right)\right\|_{L^p}\\
&\quad\lesssim\ell^{-2}  \left( 1+  \frac{1}{\ell^{L}\lambda_{q+1}^{L-2}}  \right)  \frac{\left\|\nabla\left(\eta_{(\xi)}\eta_{(\xi')}\right)\right\|_{L^p}}{\lambda_{q+1}}\\
&\quad\lesssim\frac{\sigma r^{4-\tfrac {3}{p}}}{\ell^2}\,.
\end{align*}$$

Summing in $\xi$ and $i$ we lose an additional $\ell^{-1}$ factor. By (65) this bound is consistent with (5).

Now let us consider $E_{(\xi,\xi',2)}$ for the case $\xi+\xi'=0$. Applying the identity (29) we have

$$\begin{align*}
E_{(\xi,-\xi,2)}&=\mathbb P_{\neq 0}\left(a_{(\xi)}^2\nabla \eta_{(\xi)}^2-a_{(\xi)}^2 \frac{\xi}{\mu}  \partial_t \left(\eta_{(\xi)}^2\right) \right) \\
& = \nabla\left( a_{(\xi)}^2 \mathbb P_{{\geq}\tfrac{\lambda_{q+1}\sigma}{2}}\left(\eta_{(\xi)}^2\right)\right)- \mathbb P_{\neq 0}\left(\mathbb P_{{\geq}\tfrac{\lambda_{q+1}\sigma}{2}}\left(\eta_{(\xi)}^2\right)\nabla a_{(\xi)}^2\right) \\
&\qquad- \frac{1}{\mu} \partial_t \mathbb P_{\neq 0}\left(a_{(\xi)}^2 \eta_{(\xi)}^2 \xi\right) + \frac{1}{\mu}  \mathbb P_{\neq 0}\left(\eta_{(\xi)}^2 \partial_t \left(a_{(\xi)}^2\right)\xi\right)\,. \tag{70}\end{align*}$$

Here we have used that ${\mathbb{P}}_{\neq 0} \eta_{(\xi)}^2 = {\mathbb{P}}_{\geq \tfrac{\lambda_{q+1}\sigma}{2}} \eta_{(\xi)}^2$, which holds since $\eta_{(\xi)}$ is $(\tfrac{{\mathbb{T}}}{\lambda_{q+1} \sigma})^3$-periodic. Hence, summing in $\xi$ and $i$, using that $\eta_{(\xi)}=\eta_{(-\xi)}$, pairing with the $\partial_t w^{(t)}_{q+1}$ present in (67), recalling the definition of $w^{(t)}_{q+1}$ in (50), and noting that ${\mathrm{Id}}-{\mathbb{P}}_H = \nabla \Delta^{-1} {\mathrm{div\,}}$, we obtain

$$\begin{align*}
&\sum_{i}\sum_{\xi\in \Lambda_{(i)}^+}E_{(\xi,-\xi,2)}+\partial_t w^{(t)}_{q+1} \\
&\quad =
\nabla\left(  \sum_{i}\sum_{\xi\in \Lambda_{(i)}^+}a_{(\xi)}^2 \mathbb P_{{\geq}\tfrac{\lambda_{q+1}\sigma}{2}}\left(\eta_{(\xi)}^2\right)\right)
 -\sum_{i}\sum_{\xi\in \Lambda_{(i)}^+}\mathbb P_{\neq 0}\left(\mathbb P_{{\geq}\tfrac{\lambda_{q+1}\sigma}{2}}\left(\eta_{(\xi)}^2\right)\nabla a_{(\xi)}^2\right)
 \\
&\quad- \nabla \left( \sum_{i}\sum_{\xi\in \Lambda_{(i)}^+}\frac{1}{\mu} \Delta^{-1} {\mathrm{div\,}}\partial_t \left(a_{(\xi)}^2  \eta_{(\xi)}^2 \xi\right) \right)
 +\frac{1}{\mu}  \sum_{i}\sum_{\xi\in \Lambda_{(i)}^+} {\mathbb{P}}_{\neq 0}\left(\eta_{(\xi)}^2 \partial_t \left(a_{(\xi)}^2\right) \xi\right) \, . \tag{71}\end{align*}$$

The first and third terms are pressure terms and to the remaining terms we apply the inverse divergence operator $\mathcal R$. Thus it suffices to estimate $\mathcal R$ applied to the second and the last term above. We split the second term of (71) into its summands, apply $\mathcal R$, and estimate each term individually, similarly to the estimate of $\mathcal RE_{(\xi,\xi',1)}$. Using (3.2), Lemma 4.5 and Lemma B, estimate (B), with $\lambda = \ell^{-1}$, $C_a = \ell^{-2}$, $\kappa = \tfrac{\lambda_{q+1} \sigma}{2}$, and for $b$ and $L$ sufficiently large ($L\geq 3$ and $\tfrac{b(L-2)}{16} \geq 20 L$), we obtain

$$\begin{align*}
\left\|\mathcal R\left(\mathbb P_{{\geq}\tfrac{\lambda_{q+1}\sigma}{2}}(\eta_{(\xi)}^2)\nabla a_{(\xi)}^2\right)\right\|_{L^p}&\lesssim
\frac{ 1}{\ell^2\lambda_{q+1}\sigma}\left(1+\frac{1}{\ell^L\left(\lambda_{q+1} \sigma\right)^{L-2}}\right)  \left\|\eta_{(\xi)}^2\right\|_{L^p}\lesssim\frac{ r^{3-\tfrac {3}{p}}}{\ell^2\lambda_{q+1}\sigma}
\,. \tag{72}\end{align*}$$

Summing over $\xi$ and $i$ we lose a factor of $\ell^{-1}$. Lastly, applying $\mathcal R$ to the last term on the right side of (71), and the bound on each summand is a simple consequence of (3.2) and Lemma 4.5:

$$\begin{align*}
\left\|\mathcal R\left(\frac{1}{\mu}\sum_{i}\sum_{\xi\in \Lambda_{(i)}^+} \mathbb P_{\neq 0}\left(\partial_t (a_{(\xi)}^2)\eta_{(\xi)}^2 \xi\right)\right)\right\|_{L^p}&\lesssim\frac{1}{\mu}\sum_{i}\sum_{\xi\in \Lambda_{(i)}^+}\left\|\partial_t (a_{(\xi)}^2)\eta_{(\xi)}^2 \xi\right\|_{L^p}\\
&\lesssim\frac{1}{\mu}\sum_{i}\sum_{\xi\in \Lambda_{(i)}^+}\left\|a_{(\xi)}\right\|_{C^{1}_{t,x}}\left\|a_{(\xi)}\right\|_{L^{\infty}}\left\|\eta_{(\xi)}\right\|_{L^{2p}}^2\\
&\lesssim\frac{1}{\mu}\sum_{i}\ell^{-1}\delta_{q+1}^{\tfrac12}2^ir^{3-\tfrac{3}{p}}\\
&\lesssim\frac{\ell^{-2}r^{3-\tfrac{3}{p}}}{\mu} \lesssim\frac{r^{3-\tfrac{3}{p}}}{\ell^2\lambda_{q+1}\sigma} \tag{73}\end{align*}$$

where we have used that $\lambda_{q+1}\sigma\leq \mu$. Using (65), the bounds (72) and (73) and consistent with (5), which concludes the proof of Proposition 5.

# A $L^p$ product estimate

*Proof of Lemma 3.3.* For convenience we give here the proof from (BMV17). We first consider the case $p=1$. With these assumptions we have

$$\left\|f g\right\|_{L^1} \leq \sum_j \int_{T_j} \left|fg\right|$$

$$\begin{align*}

# B Commutator estimate

*Proof of Lemma B.* We have that

$$\begin{align*}
|\nabla|^{-1} (a \; {\mathbb{P}}_{\geq \kappa} f) 
&= |\nabla|^{-1} ({\mathbb{P}}_{\leq \tfrac{\kappa}{2}} a \; {\mathbb{P}}_{\geq \kappa} f)  + |\nabla|^{-1} ({\mathbb{P}}_{\geq \tfrac{\kappa}{2}}  a \; {\mathbb{P}}_{\geq \kappa} f) \\
&=({\mathbb{P}}_{\geq \tfrac{\kappa}{2}} |\nabla|^{-1}) ({\mathbb{P}}_{\leq \tfrac{\kappa}{2}} a \; {\mathbb{P}}_{\geq \kappa} f)  + |\nabla|^{-1} ({\mathbb{P}}_{\geq \tfrac{\kappa}{2}}  a \; {\mathbb{P}}_{\geq \kappa} f)  \, . \tag{81}\end{align*}$$

Note that $\int_{{\mathbb{T}}^3} {\mathbb{P}}_{\geq \tfrac{\kappa}{2}} g(x) dx = 0$ for any function $g$, and thus the assumption that $a \, {\mathbb{P}}_{\geq \kappa} f$ has zero mean on ${\mathbb{T}}^3$, implies that ${\mathbb{P}}_{\geq \tfrac{\kappa}{2}} a \, {\mathbb{P}}_{\geq \kappa} f$ also has zero mean on ${\mathbb{T}}^3$. We then use

$$\begin{align*}

\left\||\nabla|^{-1} {\mathbb{P}}_{\geq \tfrac{\kappa}{2}} \right\|_{L^p\to L^p} \lesssim\frac{1}{\kappa}
\end{align*}$$

which is a direct consequence of the Littlewood-Paley decomposition, and the bound

$$\begin{align*}

\left\||\nabla|^{-1} {\mathbb{P}}_{\neq 0}\right\|_{L^p \to L^p} \lesssim 1
\end{align*}$$

which is a direct consequence of Schauder estimates (see (GrafakosClassical)). Combining these facts and appealing to the embedding $W^{1,4}({\mathbb{T}}^3) \subset L^\infty({\mathbb{T}}^3)$, we obtain

$$\begin{align*}
\left\||\nabla|^{-1} (a \; {\mathbb{P}}_{\geq \kappa} f)\right\|_{L^p}
&\lesssim\frac{1}{\kappa} \left\|{\mathbb{P}}_{\leq \tfrac{\kappa}{2}} a \; {\mathbb{P}}_{\geq \kappa} f\right\|_{L^p}
+ \left\|{\mathbb{P}}_{\geq \tfrac{\kappa}{2}}  a \; {\mathbb{P}}_{\geq \kappa} f\right\|_{L^p} \\
&\lesssim\left( \left\|a\right\|_{L^\infty}  + \kappa \left\|D {\mathbb{P}}_{\geq \tfrac{\kappa}{2}}a \right\|_{L^4} \right)\frac{ \left\|f\right\|_{L^p}}{\kappa} \\
&\lesssim\left( \left\|a\right\|_{L^\infty}  + \kappa^{2-L} \left\|D^L {\mathbb{P}}_{\geq \tfrac{\kappa}{2}}a \right\|_{L^4} \right)\frac{ \left\|f\right\|_{L^p}}{\kappa} \\
&\lesssim\left( \left\|a\right\|_{L^\infty}  + \kappa^2  \frac{\left\|D^L a \right\|_{L^\infty}}{\kappa^L} \right)\frac{ \left\|f\right\|_{L^p}}{\kappa}
\end{align*}$$

and the proof of (B) is concluded in view of assumption (B). ◻
